title: Collapsing Waste Fractions Without Reducing Sorting Accuracy
description: Waste sorting signs present an inviting avenue for comparison of categorisation theories as they often contain both a rule and either an abstract prototype or visual exemplars. Focus in waste sorting studies is often on increasing the number of waste fractions, but some public settings might require fewer-than-ordinary fractions. This paper investigates two approaches to reducing a waste sorting system’s granularity at a music festival: explicit combining waste fractions by merging waste signs and implicitly combining fractions by removing alternatives to ‘residual waste’. The digital sorting results are modelled as a probit regression allowing direct interpretation in terms of signal detection theory’s senstitivy and criterion parameters. The paper further compares four alternative waste sorting signs including visual exemplars to improve waste sorting accuracy for the implicitly combined waste fraction. The results suggest that explicitly combining waste fractions outperform implicit combinations – even with visual exemplars added, despite resulting in more false positives.

title: From Features to Objects: Developmental Differences in Reinforcement Learning Strategies
description: Humans constantly learn in complex environments, and a central challenge is deciding whether to attend to individual features or whole objects – a learning strategy that may shift with development. Here, we investigated developmental differences between children and adults in biases toward these two forms of learning. Participants (children aged 8–12 and adults) completed a reinforcement learning task in which both strategies had benefits, allowing us to model and directly compare them across age groups. Both groups showed clear signs of learning, but adults obtained more rewards than children. Interestingly, adults showed a clear preference for object-based learning, whereas children appeared to arbitrate equally between the two strategies. Dynamic model comparisons further showed that although both groups gradually shifted from feature-based to object-based learning over time, this transition was more pronounced in adults. Children, by contrast, relied longer on feature-based learning and focused more on features predictive of reward. Together, these findings suggest that developmental changes in reinforcement learning efficiency are driven by prolonged reliance on feature-level representations early in life, with increasing age marked by a shift toward more efficient, object-centered strategies. Importantly, these differences reflect the granularity of learned representations rather than differences in learning rate, highlighting how humans extract structure from complex reward environments across development.

title: Social media reveals population dynamics of dysphoric dreaming
description: Nightmares disrupt sleep health and predict future psychiatric diagnoses, yet reliable population estimates and their fluctuations over time are difficult to obtain. Here, we set out to test if a digital surveillance approach could be used to observe reliable estimates of nightmare frequency and dysphoric dreaming in the general population from social media posts. English-language posts from r/Dreaming, a subreddit where users share their dreams, were analyzed using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count to quantify nightmare frequency and anxious dreaming from text. An interrupted time series analysis was used to show that both nightmare frequency and dysphoric dreaming increased immediately following the World Health Organization's declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic. This observation mirrors a large body of existing work that used more traditional methods. This "digital dream surveillance" approach might offer the field of sleep medicine a low-cost and real-time system for monitoring population sleep health.

title: Mapping Extreme Deviations in Cognition to Transdiagnostic Compulsivity: A Normative Modelling Approach
description: Transdiagnostic compulsivity has been linked to reductions in model-based planning, cognitive flexibility and working memory. However, it’s unclear if these effects reflect dimensional variation or asymmetric effects at the extremes. To address this, we used normative modelling to identify extreme positive and negative deviations in cognitive performance using data from N=10,328 participants who completed three smartphone-based tasks. Individuals were stratified into model-derived cognition categories (extreme low: <10th percentile, moderate: 10th-90th percentile, extreme high: >90th percentile), and differences in compulsivity scores across groups were assessed via regression. We report disproportionately elevated compulsivity scores among participants with extreme negative deviations, but no commensurate decrease in those with extreme positive deviations. Compulsivity norms revealed disproportionally reduced cognitive performance among participants with extreme positive deviations, but no corresponding increase in those with extreme negative deviations. These findings provide a nuanced understanding of directional differences driving clinical-cognitive relationships, further refining mechanistic accounts of compulsivity.

title: Self-Control as a Mediator Between Personality Traits and Subjective Well-Being: Evidence from Three Panel Studies
description:
Objective
Research suggests that self-control may mediate the relationships between the Big Five personality traits and subjective well-being (SWB), yet its role remains unclear. 
Method
The mediating effect of self-control (measured at Time 2 (T2) on the relationships between the Big Five personality traits (measured at Time 1 (T1)) and components of SWB (measured at Time 3 (T3)) were examined in three longitudinal panel datasets of which three assessment waves were considered: HILDA (Australia, N = 11,737, Mage at T1= 46.19), SOEP (Germany, N = 1,268, Mage at T1= 52.94), and MIDUS (United States, N = 2,614, Mage at T1= 46.30). The intervals from T1 to T3 were 4 years in HILDA, 5 years in SOEP, and 20 years in MIDUS. 
Results
Self-control mediated the associations of Neuroticism and Conscientiousness with life satisfaction across all samples, and with positive and negative affect in HILDA and MIDUS samples. The mediating role of self-control varied by sex, with Extraversion demonstrating a significant pathway for women but not men in HILDA.
Conclusions
These findings indicate that self-control links personality traits to SWB, with potential implications for intervention.

title: Personal evaluation of narrator-to-story fit is a stronger predictor of audiobook enjoyment than crowd-sourced opinion.
description: Here, we report two experiments investigating how perceived narrator-to-story fit affects audiobook listening enjoyment and other listening outcomes. In a first experiment (N=400 participants), we manipulated the gender-related congruence between the expected and heard narrator of four audiobooks in a willingness-to-wait paradigm. We found that listeners were more likely to continue listening to congruent than incongruent stories, but did not enjoy them more or comprehend them more accurately. However, higher individual evaluations of narrator-to-story fit significantly increased enjoyment, while both higher individual and (aggregated) mean fit ratings predicted greater motivation to continue listening. This suggested that crowd-sourced data may be less effective than personal taste when predicting audiobook listening enjoyment. Indeed, a second experiment using a larger number of stories showed that participants’ enjoyment of audiobooks is most strongly predicted by within-sample individual fit ratings, but not by within- or between-group aggregate ratings. Our findings provide evidence to support personalisation of audiobook narration as a way to promote enjoyment of books.

title: From Courtrooms to Ballots: A Social Ecological Analysis of Anti-Trans Judicial Outcomes on Legislation, Elections, and Trans Geographic Demography
description: We applied a social ecological model to examine whether judicial decisions denying trans plaintiffs’ claims in employment discrimination cases forecast anti-trans legislative growth, and in turn, Trump support and LGBT and trans geographic demography. That is, we explore associations between anti-trans actions in three branches of government. Specifically, we coded (a) a census of trans employment discrimination judicial case outcomes (N = 124) decided from 1974 to 2021, (b) the number of anti-trans bills each state introduced, (c) state electoral support for Trump, and (d) state LGBT population density and trans geographic relocation. Supporting hypotheses, states where judges disproportionately denied trans plaintiffs’ employment discrimination claims were more likely to introduce anti-trans legislation, which in turn, was associated with increased likelihood of state electoral support for Trump, lower state LGBT population density, and greater trans geographic relocation. Refuting the notion of an independent judiciary, judicial decisions in trans employment discrimination cases forecasted the drastic growth in anti-trans legislation, and in turn, executive branch outcomes. This research suggests that a social ecological theoretical model may offer a useful framework for understanding the influences and consequences of anti-trans legislation.

title: A qualitative systematic literature review of the lived experiences of people with depersonalisation-derealisation disorder
description:
Introduction: Despite depersonalisation-derealisation being the third most commonly reported psychiatric symptom, it remains chronically understudied and poorly understood. Research into depersonalisation-derealisation disorder (DDD) is largely quantitative and remains scarce. This systematic literature review is the first review to synthesise available qualitative research about DDD lived experiences to understand the nature and impact of the disorder’s symptoms. The findings are interpreted in light of the cognitive behavioural model of DDD.  

Methods: Five electronic databases (APA PsycArticles, APA PsycInfo, CINAHL Ultimate, open dissertations, MEDLINE Ultimate) were searched alongside Google Scholar from their inception until September 2025 using a combination of search terms for depersonalisation, derealisation, lived experiences and qualitative methods. The methodological quality of studies was assessed using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme Tool for qualitative research and data was analysed using Thomas and Harden’s (2008) approach to thematic synthesis. 

Results: Twelve studies were identified as eligible for inclusion. Thematic synthesis revealed five themes across participants’ accounts: (i) Struggling to Navigate Distortions in Time and Sensory Perception; (ii) Changes in Identity, Roles and Beliefs; (iii) Navigating Societal Stigma and Altered Relationships; (iv) Negative Affective Responses: Anxiety, Numbness, Suicidality; and (v) Challenges to Daily Functioning. Most studies demonstrated high methodological quality, with only one exception. 

Discussion: The lived experiences presented in this review provide context to the impact of DDD symptoms on individuals and those around them. title: Calm but Disconnected: A Mixed-Methods Feasibility Trial of Nonviolent Communication as a Prosthetic Capability for Student Belonging
description: University students increasingly report loneliness and diminished belonging despite high levels of surface-level social contact. This paper presents a pre-registered mixed-methods feasibility trial (N = 30; 15 dyads) comparing two priming strategies for interpersonal connection during a structured dyadic interaction. Participants were randomly allocated to receive either a 15-minute Nonviolent Communication (NVC) primer — teaching the Observation–Feeling–Need–Request (OFNR) interpersonal scaffold — or a standardised 15-minute mindfulness body scan before completing the Fast Friends Procedure (Aron et al., 1997). Quantitative outcomes (Inclusion of Other in Self [IOS]; Psychological Sense of School Membership–8 [PSSM-8]; Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale [WEMWBS]) were integrated with behavioural observation (Net Safety Index [NSI]) and directed content analysis of five debrief probes within a COM-B theoretical framework (Michie et al., 2011). NVC-primed dyads showed significantly greater post-interaction interpersonal closeness than mindfulness-primed dyads (IOS: U = 160.5, p = .041, rrb = −.43, medium effect). Within-group analyses revealed large IOS gains in both conditions (r = .89 NVC; r = .68 mindfulness), while WEMWBS improvements were driven by the mindfulness arm alone (r = .82). Qualitative data identified a Masking Paradox: mindfulness produced intrapersonal calm without equivalent interpersonal capability, evidenced by higher rates of reported awkwardness (85% vs. 56%) and greater reliance on the structural safety mechanism (Veto Card used: 2 mindfulness, 0 NVC). Triangulation across three data strands yielded convergent evidence for five theoretical patterns: Perceived Safety, Masking Paradox, Intimacy Mechanic, Complementary Divergence, and Protocol Feasibility. title: Urban versus Rural Living and Health Outcomes: A Global Synthesis of Evidence Across Multiple Domains
description: Urbanization has raised urgent questions about how environmental contexts shape mental and physical health. This review synthesizes findings from 500 studies (1982–2023) on mental health, physical health, brain function, cognition, personality, and epigenetics in urban versus rural settings. In the Global North, urban living is linked to increased risks for mental disorders, particularly schizophrenia, whereas rural living is often associated with better quality of life. In the Global South, urban environments may confer mental health benefits, likely due to improved healthcare and economic opportunities. Urban populations, mostly in the North, show higher rates of obesity and cardiovascular disease, while rural groups face greater mortality risks linked to healthcare disparities. Neuroimaging studies suggest urban upbringing alters stress-related brain circuits. However, causal inferences are limited by cross-sectional designs, inconsistent definitions of “urban” and “rural,” and overrepresentation of Global North populations. Improved classification and global representation are needed to inform equitable and effective health policy.

title: Beyond Snapshots: A Systematic Review of Dyadic and Triadic Parent-Adolescent Ecological Momentary Assessment Studies Across Diverse and General Populations
description: The last decade has seen a surge in studies using Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA), where participants complete brief daily questionnaires to capture real-time experiences. While widely used to study adolescents' social-emotional processes, EMA that simultaneously assesses adolescents and their parents (i.e., dyadic and triadic designs) remains underutilized, particularly within diverse families. This gap is surprising given the proven value of dyadic EMA in studying adult relationships and its potential to elucidate contextualized family dynamics. This systematic review synthesized and critically evaluated existing EMA research in parent-adolescent dyads and triads (i.e., an adolescent and both parents) published between 2014 and 2024, examining methodological and analytical practices as well as representation of diverse populations (i.e., racial/ethnic, sexual and gender minorities, lower-SES, non-traditional family structures, and clinical populations). Following a systematic search of electronic databases, we identified 85 publications originating from 44 distinct datasets that conducted EMA in parent-adolescent dyads or triads. Substantial variability was observed across studies in the number of daily assessments, EMA days, and data-waves collected. Utilization of the multilevel and dyadic features of the data also varied: most papers fully utilized the temporal aspect (e.g., examining within-family processes), while the dyadic/triadic aspect was only partially utilized (e.g., most studies examined unidirectional effects, typically parent-to-child). Regarding populations studied, while most focused on White, non-Hispanic, highly educated samples, some targeted only minority groups (e.g., Chinese-American). However, whether within-family processes differ between populations was rarely examined. title: The skewed distribution of educational technology research - a sign of academic hegemony? An analysis of localization in scientific publications
description: Academic knowledge is interwoven with historical power structures, leading to global ine-qualities in the visibility of research, and favouring studies from the Global North. Articles from the Global North are significantly less likely to incorporate geographic markers in their titles compared to those addressing the Global South. We examine the prevalence of regional markers in the titles of 39,764 educational technology research studies from 81 Scopus-indexed journals between 2015 and 2024. Only 11.4% of study titles indicate a geo-graphical region. If so, articles from sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America show the highest localization rate, and Europe and North America the lowest. Multiple regression analysis uncovers a negative correlation between per capita GDP and localization rates, suggesting that as countries develop economically, the tendency of articles being localized decreases. Publishing conventions may thus reinforce epistemic hierarchies by favouring studies that appear to be more widely applicable, relegating others to regional relevance.

title: Revisiting Cross-Modal Matching in the Light of Luce’s Global Psychophysical Theory
description: In this high-powered replication of the classical cross-modal matching experiment by Stevens and Marks (1965, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 54, 407-411) examining loudness and brightness, we complement the traditional group-level analysis with an analysis at the individual level, and model the underlying mechanisms utilizing the theory of global psychophysics with internal references. In cross-modal matching, one typically finds a shortened range of the adjusted stimulus exhibiting a tendency towards a mid-level intensity. This well-replicated result is called regression effect.  We implement a novel Bayesian estimation of the global psychophysics model for cross-modal matching.  In a sample of seven subjects, the regression effect is found both at the aggregated and the individual level. The observed prevalent nonlinearity of the individual matching curves can be captured by the global psychophysics model.  Implications and further directions are discussed.

title: Adaptive Cognitive Control in Prospective Memory
description: Event-Based Prospective Memory (PM) requires performing a planned action upon encountering a target event. The PM decision control (PMDC) model quantifies the dual mechanisms of cognitive control (proactive and reactive, Braver, 2012) that support PM. Here, we test a key prediction of the dual-mechanisms theory: that cognitive control will shift from proactive to reactive as the need for control lessens due to PM targets being infrequent. Participants made lexical decisions (ongoing task) and were presented blocks of trials which either contained no PM targets, a high PM target frequency (19% of trials), or a low PM target frequency (5%). We fit the behavioural data with an extended version of PMDC that was augmented to specify the ongoing-task habituation and PM learning dynamics required to account for the way in which participants adapted their behaviour as a function of task practice and expected PM target frequency. PM costs (ongoing task response slowing in PM conditions relative to no PM target condition) were observed only in the high frequency condition, explained by PMDC by an increase in proactive control. PM accuracy was similar across high and low frequency conditions early in the experiment, but later an advantage emerged for the lower frequency PM task. PMDC accounted for this with stronger reactive control in low frequency condition that increased over practice. Our results confirm the prediction that control shifts from proactive to reactive with lower target event frequency, respond to recent calls from the PM literature for theory to account for across-trial dynamics.

title: Quests, Challenges, and Clinical Change: A Review and Clinical Recommendations for the Use of Therapeutically Applied Role Playing Games for people with Psychosis.
description: While the interest in Therapeutically Applied Role-Playing Games (TA-RPGs) is growing globally, there is a reluctance from clinicians and researchers to apply this intervention with people who experience psychosis. Understandably, there are concerns that a fantasy-based game will exacerbate psychotic symptoms. This review assesses the evidence relating to the risks and benefits of implementing TA-RPGs with people with a lived experienced of psychosis. Despite these concerns, there is no evidence that participation in TA-RPGs exacerbates symptoms for those who experience psychosis. Instead, emerging evidence highlights the benefits of engaging in TA-RPG interventions for many participants, regardless of the presence of psychotic symptoms. We highlight the need for more transparency and research in this area to reduce the research-to-practice gap and address stigma for those experiencing psychosis. Finally, we provide clinical recommendations to increase safety when implementing TA-RPGs with this population.

title: Validating an abridged version of Planets and Pirates  conditioned punishment task
description: The Planets and Pirates task is used to investigate individual differences in learning about the adverse consequences of one’s actions. However, the original paradigm is relatively lengthy, which may limit its utility in time-sensitive and clinical research settings. The present study evaluated an abridged version of the task by directly comparing performance between the original and abridged formats in an undergraduate student sample. Consistent with prior findings (Gaetani et al., 2025; Jean-Richard-dit-Bressel., 2021, 2023), three distinct phenotypes of human punishment learning emerged from both tasks: “sensitive” individuals who adapted behaviour through experience, “unaware” individuals who failed to correctly learn through direct experience but corrected their behaviour following an information intervention, and “compulsive” phenotype who persisted in punished responding despite direct experience and informational intervention. Phenotypic differences were not attributable to variations in task engagement or outcome valuations. Rather, insensitivity to punishment reflected difficulties in correctly attributing outcomes to actions and integrating causal knowledge into action selection. Importantly, the abridged task demonstrated higher overall engagement and lower attrition compared to levels observed in the original task. These findings indicate that the abridged Planets and Pirates task retains sensitivity to detecting core markers of punishment insensitivity while offering a more suitable format for large-scale studies and clinical research.

title: Toward a Formalization of Human Intuitive Theories of Bodily Pain
description: Pain is a subjective experience that people often communicate through words. How do observers, from family members to medical professionals, interpret these reports? We propose that people use causal inference to infer someone else's subjective pain experience, treating the pain experience as an unobservable latent variable and the report as one of several sources of observations. We formalized this as Bayesian inference over a causal model of bodily pain and tested it against human judgments on naturalistic stimuli drawn from Reddit posts. Critically, the model is stimulus-computable, taking as input exactly what participants see. The model quantitatively predicted human judgments about pain intensity and appropriate painkiller dosage and generalized across different kinds of pain (e.g., from headaches to finger burns). Furthermore, the model captured individual differences correlated with people's explicit beliefs about how best to assess pain. This work takes a first step toward a scientific understanding of folk intuitive theories of pain.

title: Psychometric Evaluation of Online Sexual Abuse Indicators in the UNICEF Disrupting Harm Project
description:
This analysis examined the psychometric properties of nine items related to online sexual exploitation and abuse, as well as follow-up questions on disclosures and reporting, from the Disrupting Harm questionnaire. Both two- and three-factor structures were identified through exploratory factor analyses and validated using confirmatory factor analyses. Each model demonstrated good fit, with adequate item loadings and no cross-loadings. 
The three-factor model aligned conceptually with pre-registered factors, labelled ‘risk of sexual exploitation’ (four items), ‘risk of sexual abuse’ (three items), and ‘risk of sexual harassment’ (two items). In contrast, the two-factor model combined ‘risk of sexual abuse’ and ‘risk of sexual harassment’ into a single factor, ‘risk of sexual harassment and abuse’ (five items), with ‘risk of sexual exploitation’ (four items) remaining separate.
Reliability for the two-item ‘risk of sexual harassment’ factor in the three-factor model was low, consistent with psychometric literature indicating that three items are typically required for reliable measurement. Consequently, further analyses, including measurement invariance and item response theory, focused on the two-factor model, which demonstrated good reliability for all factors. The two-factor model showed strict invariance across sex, strong invariance across age, and strong invariance across countries after applying a log transformation to resolve convergence issues.
Item response theory on the two-factor model indicated that the factors were most informative at average trait levels, providing the highest measurement precision for respondents with moderate levels of responses across each of the nine items. title: Switching to an Allocentric Spatial Reference Frame Incurs Distinct Cognitive Processing Costs
description: The ability to acquire, recall, and flexibly use information from first-person (egocentric) and map-like (allocentric) reference frames is essential for human wayfinding and thus, daily life. Prevailing models of the neural systems that support the representation and coordination between reference frames suggest that switching back-and-forth should result in either lower accuracy, slower response time (RT), or both. However, predictions of these models have not been adequately tested for spatial memory of large-scale, naturalistic environments. Inspired by previous work on task switching, we developed a novel task in which participants performed a spatial memory switching task that included trials in both egocentric and allocentric reference frames. Participants learned a large virtual neighborhood by navigating to various target stores. They then completed runs of the memory task, with approximately equal numbers of egocentric and allocentric trials. Critically, we manipulated whether the same reference frame was repeated or switched on a trial-to-trial basis to determine whether there is a cost associated with changing reference frames. Results showed no significant differences in spatial memory accuracy across conditions but significantly slower RTs for switching trials. Importantly, this reference frame switch cost was only observed for egocentric-to-allocentric switching (not vice versa) relative to all other conditions. These findings suggest that the cognitive process of reference frame switching is asymmetric, which went against our predictions from neural models. Future neuroimaging studies to test predictions generated by our results will provide crucial insight into human spatial memory function.

title: Content Validation Using Natural Language Processing: A Comparative Examination of Models for Multi-Item and Single-Item Measures
description: Content validation, the assessment of whether measurement items adequately capture their intended constructs, is essential to scale development in organizational research but remains resource-intensive when conducted through conventional human-rating procedures. Natural language processing (NLP) offers a scalable complement for estimating definitional correspondence and distinctiveness, yet no study has systematically compared the full range of available approaches against direct human validity judgments across both multi-item and single-item measurement formats. The present study evaluates 16 NLP models spanning five architectural families (statistical models, static word embeddings, contextual sentence embeddings, task-specific interaction models and large language models) using two independent human-rated benchmark datasets. Results indicated that no single approach dominated across validity components or measurement formats, and that computational complexity was neither necessary nor sufficient for predictive accuracy. For multi-item correspondence, contextual sentence embeddings achieved top-group accuracy alongside supervised content-validation models; the choice of similarity metric substantially moderated performance for static embeddings. For multi-item distinctiveness, a broad upper group spanning all major architectural families achieved statistically indistinguishable accuracy. Single-item correspondence revealed a task-imposed performance ceiling with no architectural advantage. Practical recommendations are derived for each use case, prioritizing reproducibility, interpretability, and generalizability alongside predictive accuracy. A freely available web application implementing the recommended pipeline is introduced.

title: The Strength of Target Representations Drives Mnemonic Discrimination at Extended Delays
description: Mnemonic discrimination, or the ability to distinguish between similar remembered experiences, is critical for episodic memory and is dependent on the computational process of pattern separation. Prior work with tasks that place high demands on mnemonic discrimination such as the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST) has focused on short retention intervals and it remains unclear how mnemonic discrimination evolves over longer delays. To address this gap in understanding, we examined MST performance at delays ranging from a few minutes to seven days in two experiments. Consistent with prior forgetting literature, both recognition of repeated items and discrimination of similar lures declined with delay. In the immediate delay condition, the similarity of lure stimuli to targets drove discrimination performance, with more similar lures eliciting false alarms and less similar lures eliciting correct rejections, as reflected in the lure discrimination index (LDI). This graded relationship was attenuated or absent at delays longer than one day. However, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses revealed preserved discrimination across delays and target-lure similarity levels. Additionally, we observed an inversion of the typical confidence-accuracy relationship for lure trials at longer delays, with low-confidence responses more likely to be correct especially for high-similarity lures. Together these findings reflect the influence of the strength of target representations on lure discrimination: strong target representations lead to high-confidence correct rejections of low-similarity lures but also to high-confidence false alarms to high-similarity lures. As target representations weaken over extended delays, false alarms to high-similarity lures become less likely while low-similarity lures were more likely to be called “new”. This is the first demonstration of how mnemonic discrimination in the MST changes over extended delays.

title: Preregistration records do not reliably reflect the true state of psychology meta-analyses
description: Meta-analysis preregistration is intended to promote transparency and reduce research waste. However, it is largely unknown whether preregistration records accurately reflect the actual state of research, and how many preregistered meta-analyses are ultimately published in the field of psychology. We searched PROSPERO for preregistrations of psychology meta-analyses registered between 2011 and 2021 (n = 1137), verified publication status through systematic search, and contacted corresponding authors of unpublished registrations (n = 358) to obtain information on reasons for delays and discontinuations. We found that PROSPERO status labels were systematically inaccurate: 57% of records labelled "ongoing" were already published, and publication rates varied by registration status (Completed: 94%; Ongoing: 59%; Discontinued: 9%). Among 80 survey respondents, resource limitations were the primary reasons for project discontinuation (lack of time: 47%; lack of personnel: 11%; lack of funding: 7%) and preregistration quality showed no association with publication likelihood. Altogether, these findings suggest that PROSPERO registrations in psychology frequently fail to reflect the true status of a meta-analysis, undermining their value as a transparency tool, and that resource limitations frequently lead to meta-analysis abandonment. We recommend that journals and funders require registration updates at publication to reduce the accumulation of inaccurate and abandoned records.

title: What’s on Their For You Page? A Large-Scale Computational Approach to Analyzing Adolescents’ TikTok Archives Through Hashtag Topic Modeling
description: Short-form video platforms like TikTok play a central role in adolescents’ lives, yet little is known about the actual content they engage with. This study presents a large-scale, computational approach to analyze adolescents’ TikTok feeds using hashtag-based topic modeling applied to user-donated archives from 102 Dutch adolescents (ages 15–19). Using BERTopic, we identified 304 coherent topics, organized them into 32 higher-order content categories, and validated both through a structured human validation study. Analyses reveal that adolescents’ feeds are dominated by entertainment and leisure content, with ‘Media productions,’ ‘Sports,’ ‘Style and appearance,’ ‘Hobbies,’ and ‘Gaming’ as the most prevalent categories. At the same time, there is marked individual variation: niche areas such as K-pop, anime, and specific fandoms are central to some users’ feeds. Latent profile analysis identified six distinct, gendered content-consumption profiles. Together, the findings shed light on adolescents’ TikTok exposure, revealing predominantly benign but highly personalized media diets in which appearance-focused content stands out as a potential risk domain. In all, our approach offers a scalable, efficient way to map short-form video content. Linking these maps to individual users’ media diets opens new possibilities for examining how different content patterns relate to user experiences and outcomes.

title: Effectiveness of a School-based Workshop Promoting Mental Health on Adolescents Mental Health Literacy and Emotional Self-Efficacy
description:
Theoretical background: Mental health crisis in adolescents is a growing concern in society and research. Because of the high prevalence of mental disorders during adolescence and the long waiting times for access to therapeutic services, low-threshold, school-based prevention programs are needed that empower adolescents to actively advocate for their mental health. The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of a one-day school-based mental health workshop on mental health literacy (MHL) and emotional self-efficacy (ESE) within a quasi-randomized delayed cross-over design. 

Method: Data was collected from 868 students (age: 14-17 years, 39.3% female) in six schools between March 2024 and February 2025 at three data assessment points. Participants in the intervention group (n1 = 365 (M₁ = 14.8 (0.86), 54.8% female) participated in a one-day school-based mental health workshop provided by the organization Kopfsachen e.V. between the baseline-assessment (T0), 2-3 weeks before the workshop and the post-assessment (T1) directly after the workshop. There was a follow-up assessment (T2) around six months after the baseline (T0). Participants in the waitlist-control group (n2 = 503 (M₂ = 15.0(0.85)) participated at all three assessments and received the workshop after the follow-up assessment (T2).

title: Patterns of registered and self-reported sleep problems in young adults with different histories of childhood adversity
description:
Background: Sleep problems are increasing among young adults, with those experiencing childhood adversity particularly at risk. This study provides a comprehensive overview of sleep problems in young adults following multifaceted trajectories of childhood adversity, while emphasizing the transdiagnostic nature of sleep problems.

Methods: Register data on 1,276,831 individuals were supplemented with nested survey data on 36,873 participants. Childhood adversity (ages 0-16) was operationalized using previously derived trajectories: low adversity, early life material deprivation, persistent material deprivation, loss or threat of loss, and high adversity. Sleep problems (ages 16-30) were assessed through prescriptions, diagnoses, and self-reported data. Survival models were used to estimate associations between childhood adversity and sleep problems. Co-occurrence of sleep and mental health problems were explored, and confirmatory factor analysis was used to model self-reported sleep impairment across adversity groups.

Findings: Childhood adversity was associated with sleep problems, with prevalences of 8∙2%, 10∙4%, 10∙8%, 13∙6%, and 20∙1% across the five adversity groups. Risk was highest in the high adversity (HR 2∙37; 95% CI 2∙32–2∙43) and loss or threat of loss (1∙71; 1∙68–1∙74) groups vs. low adversity. Sleep problems most commonly involved sleep medication prescriptions only (49%) but also co-occurred with mental disorders (43%). The high adversity and loss or threat of loss groups showed higher variation in self-reported sleep impairment and higher proportions above the 80th percentile compared with other groups.

title: “It Feels Like We are an Outsider”: Understanding Barriers and Creating Opportunities for Fathers’ Engagement in Parenting Programs
description: Becoming a father entails significant psychological adaptations that impact fathers’ well-being and mental health, but also that of their partners and children. As such, structured parenting programs may play an important role in supporting fathers during this transition. However, fathers remain underrepresented in these programs, and studies consistently report challenges in recruiting and engaging them. These difficulties suggest a potential misalignment between parenting programs and fathers’ needs, expectations, and sociocultural contexts, often shaped by their broader experiences with family- and health-related services. This study aims to explore how Portuguese fathers perceive and position themselves in relation to parenting programs, and to identify the social, cultural, and institutional factors that shape their engagement and non-engagement. We conducted four focus groups with 16 fathers who had at least one biological child under five years old. The focus groups were moderated by two psychologists (one male and one female) and followed a semi-structured script. Using reflexive thematic analysis, six themes were developed: fathers as secondary parents – experiences and perceptions of exclusion; generational gaps; gap between service awareness and willingness to engage; perceived legitimacy of fathers in parenting support spaces; seeking a place of belonging; design elements supporting fathers’ engagement. Overall, fathers’ engagement emerges as a contextually embedded process shaped by institutional practices, cultural expectations, and perceived legitimacy. Enhancing participation may entail fostering inclusive environments that recognize fathers as central caregivers. This calls for broader transformations of cultural and institutional frameworks that shape parenting support from the earliest stages of a father’s parenthood trajectory.

title: How and when to implement self-efficacy interventions to maximize the benefits of virtual reality exposure therapy for fear of heights
description: Strategies aimed to enhance self-efficacy (SE), such activation and evaluation as mastery experiences and verbal persuasion (i.e. positive performance feedback) may promote exposure therapy. Here, we evaluated the effects of two strategies to boost SE administered during and/or after a one-session virtual reality exposure therapy (VRET) for fear of heights. Height-fearful participants (N = 83) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: VRET alone, VRET combined with SE enhancement via positive performance feedback during VRET, VRET combined with post-exposure SE via mastery experience activation and evaluation, or VRET combining both SE enhancement strategies. Subjective, behavioral, and psychophysiological indices of height fear and general SE were assessed from pre- to post-intervention and at 3-month follow-up. Across conditions, height fear and avoidance decreased while behavioral approach increased with effects largely maintained at follow-up. Changes over time were largely comparable across conditions, however, participants receiving post-exposure mastery experience activation and evaluation showed a stronger decrease in subjective height avoidance compared to the condition that received SE enhancement during VRET. Notably, participants receiving positive performance feedback during VRET showed the least improvement (across several outcome measures). Our results indicate that post-exposure activation and evaluation of mastery experiences might be more suitable to promote VRET outcome in height fear in comparison to positive performance feedback during VRET. These findings provide novel perspectives on the potential use of SE enhancement as a supplementary strategy to augment exposure therapy and highlight potential effects of timing. This study was preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT05824884).

title: Social cognition, imitation, and sensory processing difficulties in extremely preterm-born children at six years of age
description: This study compared children born extremely preterm (EPT, before 28 weeks of gestation) with full-term children (FT) on social-cognitive abilities, sensorimotor function, socioemotional behavior, and sensory processing. Fifty-three EPT and 34 FT children aged 6 to 7 underwent standardized assessments of Affect Recognition, Theory of Mind, and Imitating Hand Positions, and parents completed validated questionnaires. EPT children showed weaker theory-of-mind abilities, greater difficulty with imitation, and more sensory processing problems than their FT peers. The findings highlight the need for research to understand the mechanisms behind these difficulties and to develop targeted interventions to improve long-term outcomes for EPT children.

title: Decision-making under risk and substance use experimentation among adolescents
description:
Background and aims
Decision-making processes have been linked to substance use frequency and related problems, yet less is known about how decision-making under explicit risk relates to early substance use experimentation during adolescence. This study examined whether decision-making under explicit risk predicts the likelihood of substance use experimentation (low-level alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis use) across adolescence.
Design
Longitudinal cohort study using mixed-effects logistic regression models.
Setting
Data were drawn from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, a multi-site longitudinal cohort from across 21 research sites in the United States.
Participants
A total of 4,320 adolescents aged 10–17 years with available decision-making and substance use data between Year 2 (mean age 11.5, SD 0.66) through Year 6 (mean age 15.6, SD 0.69) were included in the analyses.
Measurements
Substance use experimentation (past-year alcohol sip, nicotine puff, and cannabis use) data collected annually were extracted for Year 2 through Year 6. Decision-making under explicit risk was measured using the Game of Dice Task (GDT) net score assessed at Year 2 and Year 4.
Findings
Safer decision-making (higher GDT net score) was associated with lower odds of alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis experimentation across substances. A one standard deviation increase in GDT net score was associated with lower odds of alcohol sipping (adjusted OR = 0.89, 95% CI: 0.80–0.98, p = 0.022), nicotine use (OR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.52–0.95, p = 0.023), and cannabis use (OR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.31–0.84, p = 0.008). The interaction between GDT net score and age was significant for alcohol and cannabis models, indicating that the protective association between safer decision-making and substance use experimentation diminished as adolescents grew older.
Conclusions
Decision-making under explicit risk is associated with the likelihood of substance use experimentation across adolescence. Ado

title: Identifying and repairing mismatches between metadata and actual participant identifiers in CHILDES
description: Child Language Data Exchange System (CHILDES) is a large corpus of transcribed child speech covering many languages. In this brief analysis, I describe mismatches between participant identifiers between direct access to CHILDES and the R package childesr. I provide a file to correctly re-link childesr data to actual participant identifiers.

title: Preferences for speech governance are polarized across 40 countries
description: The dilemma of balancing freedom of expression against limiting the spread of misinformation defines speech governance in today's information ecosystems. Yet, we lack cross-cultural, systematic evidence on how citizens prefer to solve this dilemma and why. To measure citizens’ preferences for speech governance, we surveyed people in 40 countries across ten world regions (N = 47,719; representative for age, gender, and political ideology). People are nearly evenly split between protecting free expression (51%) and preventing misinformation from spreading (49%). However, we find that this preference is politically polarized: in 32 out of 40 countries, right-leaning participants prioritize protecting free expression more than left-leaning participants (55% vs. 48%). This polarization pattern is amplified by political interest: The more interested in politics participants are, the more right-leaning participants support free speech and left-leaning participants want to prevent misinformation from spreading. These results showcase how difficult it is for people across the world to find balancing free speech against reducing misinformation. Moreover, these results also identify what could be a new cleavage of ideological polarization that has direct implications for governing expression in information ecosystems.

title: "AI Psychosis” as folie à 1.1:AI-induced delusion and trust in Large Language Models
description: The advent of chatbot applications for LLMs like ChatGPT has led to a novel psychiatric phenomenon popularly called “AI psychosis”. Excessive LLM-use appears to trigger in the user the acquisition of delusions about the LLM, the user, or the world. More appropriately called AI-induced delusion, I argue that this phenomenon is not as novel as it appears. Rather, it parallels the already known phenomenon of folie à deux or induced delusion where a person with a delusion communicates and transmits their delusion to another person in a close, isolated social relationship. A key social epistemological mechanism for folie à deux is the deep trust in these close relationships. There is a philosophical debate about whether trust in AI systems is even possible, given that they are no agents. The phenomenon of AI-induced delusion shows that trust in LLMs is indeed possible. However, these delusions result from a conflation of interpersonal and mere pragmatic trust. These and other harms resulting from the conflation of different senses of “trust” means that we should nevertheless stop talking of “trust” in the context of extant AI systems in order to avoid this harmful confusion.

title: Why Some Words Stick and Others Fade: A Neurocognitive Perspective on Vocabulary Learning
description: Research on word learning and memory often treats words as interchangeable, overlooking how linguistic features shape encoding and recall. In this review, we advance a neurocognitive-linguistic perspective on word memorability that integrates behavioral, linguistic, and neuroscience evidence to explain why some words “stick” while others fade. We synthesize findings on how familiarity, frequency, concreteness, emotional valence and arousal, phonological structure, and semantic distinctiveness influence word learning and retention. We link these features to several underlying neural mechanisms—including amygdala-hippocampal coupling, sensorimotor cortical engagement, and inferior frontal and anterior temporal hubs—and situate them within predictive and embodied frameworks of language. These insights help to refine theories of word memorability and carry practical implications. We connect basic mechanisms to educational practice (evidence-based vocabulary selection, gesture- and rhythm-based scaffolding, adaptive digital learning) and to clinical rehabilitation (aphasia and dementia interventions that leverage high-imageability, emotionally meaningful or dense-neighborhood items, and multimodal encoding).  Finally, we argue for integrating linguistic and neurocognitive determinants into computational and theoretical models of word learning to improve predictions of memorability and support more personalized approaches to language instruction and rehabilitation.

title: How to Measure Machiavellianism? A Psychometric Evaluation of Six Scales
description: Recently, several new Machiavellianism (Mach) scales have been developed to overcome psychometric issues of classical scales such as the Mach IV (Christie & Geis, 1970). The growing number of scales has made it challenging for researchers to select an appropriate Mach measure. The current study evaluated the psychometric properties of six contemporary Mach scales—the TDMS, FFMI-SSF, MAAQ, M4, M7, and SD4 Mach— using data from 1,293 participants in the GIPO project (Grosz et al., 2025). We tested their factor structures using the simulation-cum-ROC approach for model fit cutoffs, assessed reliability estimates via McDonald's ω, examined measurement precision using graded response models, and investigated construct and criterion validity through correlations with self-report measures and incentivized behavioral measures of cheating and prosocial behavior. Expert expectations about correlation magnitudes were collected and used as benchmarks for equivalence testing and the quantifying construct validity procedure. None of the six proposed factor structures met the simulation-derived model fit cutoffs. Across reliability and validity analyses, the M4 emerged as the most psychometrically favorable scale overall, combining the highest omega total (.90) and IRT-based marginal reliability (.88) with good congruence with expert-expected correlation patterns. The TDMS and MAAQ are recommended as alternatives for researchers interested in the two-dimensional structure of Mach, as both exhibited acceptable performance in validity and reliability analyses. The FFMI-SSF warrants caution: The nomological networks of the Agency and Planfulness subscales diverged substantially from expert expectations for Mach. The present findings provide a foundation for more informed measurement selection in empirical Mach research.

title: Trade-off between performance and human-like perception in face recognition models
description: Deep learning models for face recognition are widely adopted in cognitive neuroscience, yet it is not well understood whether their excellent performance means they “see” faces like humans. Here, we collected a relatively large dataset of human face-similarity judgments to assess how well prominent face recognition models align with human perception. We found that models with high — but not the highest — recognition performance are often best aligned with human similarity judgments. We further tested to what extent a linear transformation could better align model representations with human perceptual similarity. Models with superior recognition performance benefited the least from this transformation, suggesting a deeper mismatch with human perception. Notably, the transformation reduced recognition performance for higher-performing models but gave low-performing models a slight recognition boost. Overall, our results indicate that a trade-off exists between recognition ability and human-like perceptual similarity. This may inform future work on developing more human-like models.

title: Psychometric Properties of the Seattle-Groningen Memory Assessment in Healthy Adults
description: Brief assessments are increasingly important for scalable and accessible measurement of cognitive function. The Seattle-Groningen Memory Assessment (SGMA) is an accessible memory test that quantifies individual differences in the speed of forgetting through a computational model. Unlike traditional outcome-based screening tools, the SGMA derives a mechanistic memory score from both response accuracy and response latency during an 8-minute session. Despite promising clinical and research applications, the psychometric properties of the SGMA have not been systematically evaluated. In the present study, 100 healthy young adults completed two SGMA sessions spaced approximately two weeks apart, alongside seven neuropsychological tests from the Amsterdam Cognition Scan (ACS) and questionnaires assessing depression, anxiety, and stress. The SGMA memory score showed moderate concurrent validity with ACS declarative memory measures and good discriminant validity with respect to attention, processing speed, executive functioning, and affective symptoms. Test--retest reliability was moderate to good (ICC3 = 0.68), and practice effects on the memory score were minimal and well below the minimal detectable change, supporting the suitability of the SGMA for repeated administration. Together, these findings establish the SGMA as a psychometrically sound and repeatable brief memory assessment with strong potential for both research and clinical applications.

title: Modeling Working Memory Capacity in Sentence Processing with Lossy-Context Surprisal
description:
Understanding how comprehenders interpret linguistic input in real time has long been a focus of sentence processing research. 
The recently-proposed Resource-Rational Lossy-context Surprisal (RR-LCS) model can be applied for making predictions at the level of individual readers: it predicts that individuals with low working memory capacity (WMC) have a lossy representation of the previous context and may therefore experience high surprisal at a long-distance dependency, while individuals with high WMC will experience a lower surprisal effect as this dependent to them may still be highly predictable from previous context. To date, these predictions have not been empirically tested. Here, we evaluate them using a controlled A-Maze task (Experiment 1) and an analysis of reading more naturalistic text based on the InDiCo corpus (Experiment 2). In Experiment 1, we investigated how WMC influences sentence processing across short, long, and very long dependency conditions. The results revealed that low-WMC participants initially showed a strong locality effect between the short and long conditions, which decreased over time due to adaptation. High-WMC participants demonstrated locality effects between both the short-long and long-very long conditions from the start, with these effects gradually diminishing as their memory allocation became more efficient. These findings align with the RR-LCS model's predictions, showing that high-WMC individuals maintained larger context sizes, such that they could more easily process long-distance dependencies, whereas low-WMC individuals, constrained by smaller context sizes, experienced pronounced locality effects. Experiment 2 confirmed that WMC modulates sensitivity to lossy-context surprisal (LCS), with LCS improving model fit particularly strongly for low-WMC participants.  These findings underscore the significance of individual differences in WMC for processing complex syntactic structures. By combining experimental data with com

title: Intuitive judgments of strangers are more popular but not more accurate than deliberate ones
description: Popular advice in media and self-help literature encourages people to trust their intuition when forming impressions of strangers. We tested this widespread lay belief by examining whether intuitive judgments are preferred over deliberate ones and whether such preferences are justified by differences in accuracy. In Study 1 (n = 401), participants from the general population reported using intuition more frequently, preferring it, and expressing greater confidence in it compared to deliberate reasoning when judging strangers. In Study 2, we analyzed 21,739 judgments from 380 users of the quiz app “Who Knows,” who inferred personality-related characteristics from short video introductions. Judgment mode was experimentally manipulated within persons across multiple game rounds. While intuitive judgments were again preferred, accuracy did not differ between conditions. Thus, although intuition is favored when judging strangers, it does not yield higher accuracy but may still be adaptive by achieving comparable accuracy with less time.

title: Adaptation and Validation of the Spanish version of the Perceived Occupational Stress Scale: Evidence from Factor Structure, validity, and Nomological Network
description:
Work is a double-edged sword. It fosters well-being but it is also linked to stress and burnout.  Recognizing that stress is ubiquitous and best understood encompassing both the objective and subjective perspective, this study focuses on evaluating the psychometric properties of the Spanish adaptation of the Perceived Occupational Stress Scale (POSS). In Study 1, we translated and back-translated the POSS and administered it to 675 Spanish individuals. The Spanish POSS showed strong internal reliability (α = 0.903) and a good fit with the proposed factor structure (CFI = 0.946, RMSEA = 0.206, SRMR = 0.031). Study 2 explores the impact of faking on participants' responses using an experimental design. Our findings underscore the significance of work-related factors, such as mistreatment and lack of appreciation, in predicting faking behavior. In Study 3, we delved into the nomological network of the POSS by examining correlations with related psychological variables. Notably, we only found positive correlations between perceived occupational stress and measures of work engagement and psychosocial factors.
Overall, the Spanish POSS demonstrates strong validity and reliability, closely mirroring the original scale. As an EU-compliant tool, it effectively assesses perceived occupational stress, enhancing organizational support evaluations and deepening our understanding of occupational well-being.

title: Language as infrastructure for human intelligence in Large Language Models
description: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed our understanding of artificial intelligence and challenged traditional conceptualizations of intelligence itself. During recent years, LLMs have demonstrated not merely imitation or mechanical combinations, but a profound internalization of linguistic frameworks that enables them to produce responses often indistinguishable from those generated by humans. This internalization compels us to reconsider the nature of intelligence and its manifestation in both human and artificial agents. In this theoretical paper, we argue that LLMs reflect not artificial but human intelligence deeply embedded in linguistic frameworks, arising from extensive training on human language datasets. We argue that language serves as a distributed intelligence infrastructure – a virtual container for many aspects of human intelligence that extends beyond the confines of individual biological brains. Intelligence, particularly in the context of language and LLMs, can be understood as an emergent phenomenon extracted from large-scale linguistic data. This theoretical framework contributes to cognitive science theories emphasizing distributed cognition and providing а novel perspective on the relationships between language and intelligence in both biological and artificial agents. Through synthesis of evidence from computational linguistics, mechanistic interpretability, and emergent capabilities research, we demonstrate that LLMs exhibit genuine human intelligence rather than mere statistical mimicry.

title: The use of motor imagery in geriatric rehabilitation : a case report before a cardiac surgery
description:
Introduction : This case illustrates the use of motor imagery in prehabilitation for an old patient with severe aortic insufficiency in the context of ischemic heart disease. Due to contraindications to preoperative exercise, no physical activity had been initiated. However, the worsening of his functional limitations led us to consider adaptations starting the preoperative phase.
Diagnosis : The patient presented with moderately impaired motor performance, including muscle weakness, cardiorespiratory deconditioning, and preserved walking ability. His motor imagery abilities were good.
Intervention and results : An intervention combining physical exercise (25%) and motor imagery (75%) was implemented during the 4 weeks prior to surgery. After surgery, a slight decline in motor performance, consistent with the documented postoperative trajectory, was noted. Adherence to the program was excellent.
Conclusion : This case demonstrates the feasibility of integrating motor imagery as a prehabilitation tool, offering a safe option for at-risk patients.

title: Rebuilding HiTOP from the ground up: Symptom-level analyses and a revised mapping to the DSM
description: The evidence for the structure of the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) model relies heavily on analyses of correlations among DSM diagnoses, which entrenches some of their limitations. In this study, we deconstructed the mental disorders covered in HiTOP into individual symptoms—with personality disorders represented via item-level assessment of the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders facets—and rebuilt the HiTOP model from the ground up. Participants self-selected into an online mental health study and were randomly split into primary (n = 11,762) and hold-out (n = 3,000) samples to identify a robust hierarchy of empirically derived constructs in the results, ranging from symptoms and syndromes to very broad ‘superspectra’ of psychopathology. In each sample, both hierarchical clustering and hierarchical principal components analyses were used; the final hierarchical structure was derived based on points of cross-sample and cross-method agreement. The resulting model was remarkably similar to the HiTOP model, including nearly all of the same subfactors, spectra, and superspectra—albeit with some reorganisation in the structure. The inclusion of broad hypomania/disinhibition and pathological introversion dimensions represented the most prominent differences compared to the current higher-order structure of HiTOP. The detailed lower-order constructs found here also mirrored many of the existing components and traits in HiTOP, as well as indicating some potential areas for revision. Finally, we re-mapped the disorders included in the Structured Clinical Interview for the DSM-5 onto the new model. Overall, the results suggest that the structural foundations of the HiTOP model are largely sound.

title: Environmental regularities shape visual search strategy selection
description: Visual search can be guided by multiple strategies, some of them relying on bottom-up salience, others on top-down expectations. However, little is known about how we arbitrate between these strategies. Here, we tested whether environmental regularities that incentivize different strategies can influence this arbitration. Participants performed a visual search task in which targets appeared in one of two color-defined groups of items whose relative sizes varied across trials. Because smaller groups are more visually salient, prioritizing them constitutes a bottom-up search strategy, and prioritizing the larger group requires top-down control. By manipulating the probability that the target appeared in each group, we created environments in which abstract structural properties of the display (the relative size of the groups) incentivized different strategies. Participants adapted their search strategy to these abstract regularities, but in an asymmetric fashion. Reliance on salient minority groups readily increased when it was advantageous, whereas people only became willing to prioritize the majority group when alternative salience-based cues were minimized. These results suggest that visual search strategies are shaped by environmental statistics, but their adoption is constrained by the cognitive costs of overriding bottom-up salience.

title: Beliefs without Strong Supporting Evidence: Associations with Personality Items
description: Beliefs without strong supporting evidence (BWSSE), such as conspiracy theories and pseudoscientific beliefs, are increasingly common, and their growing prevalence may have negative consequences for society. The design of more effective interventions to mitigate the spread of BWSSE may depend on understanding the personality characteristics associated with different belief types. To meet this goal, this study optimized components from a BWSSE questionnaire with respect to overlap with the Big Five Aspect Scale (BFAS), which assesses personality. Data from 417 participants who completed the BWSSE questionnaire and BFAS within standard completion times were analyzed using a multivariate statistical method to identify how individual BFAS items, rather than aggregate domain scores, were associated with the BWSSE questionnaire components optimized for overlap with the BFAS. We found that New Age beliefs were associated with creativity and emotional sensitivity (primarily items from the Openness and Agreeableness domains), Science beliefs with a preference for order, routine and systematic thinking (primarily items from the Conscientiousness and Intellect domains), Traditional Religion with respect for authority and a less expansive vocabulary (primarily items from the Agreeableness and Intellect domains), and Conspiracy Theories with enjoying conflict and easily becoming angered and agitated (primarily items from the Neuroticism domain). Different belief types were associated with distinct combinations of individual BFAS items that crossed BFAS domains, highlighting within-domain dissociations that are obscured when using aggregate domain scores. These belief-personality associations, combined with reasons for holding BWSSE, should be considered when developing strategies to reduce misinformation and promote evidence-based reasoning.

title: An energy-gradient theory of embedded predictions in the brain
description:
